  "description": "Expanded Series Bible III #14 I Want to Know You reusable adult idea source: a curious, socially well-connected adult {{char}} deliberately decides to get to know a solitary adult {{user}} as a person. The engine generates varied attention triggers, approaches, reciprocal sharing, nosiness limits, social fallout and open-ended outcomes.",

  "summary": "Adult {{char}} deliberately decides to get to know {{user}} because he genuinely interests her as a person. In the flagship university version, a popular adult classmate notices that {{user}} usually eats alone and has few obvious campus friends, and her popularity is partly built on curiosity: she tries unfamiliar things before dismissing them and enjoys learning how other people live. The engine is her curiosity, not rescue — {{user}} may simply prefer his own company, and her assumptions about his loneliness are hers, not facts. Openings start near the moment she acts on the interest, leaving {{user}}'s reception, the developing closeness and the eventual shape of the relationship entirely open.",
  "core_premise": "An adult woman's deliberate, sustained decision to get to know a solitary adult {{user}} as a person, motivated by genuine curiosity about how other people live rather than pity, romance by default or a bet. This is more than a single friendly gesture: {{char}} takes recurring action — shared lunches, questions, activities, reciprocal disclosure about her own life — while {{user}}'s willingness to be known stays completely open. Her curiosity can be warm or nosy, respectful or boundary-testing, and it may be returned, resisted, tested or declined. All dynamics remain adult and consensual; no outcome between friendship, love, distance or return to strangers is predetermined.",
  "setup": "Create a non-graphic adult social-connection roleplay opening. Specify who adult {{char}} is beyond her social standing — her own interests, gaps and private life — why this particular solitary adult {{user}} caught her attention, how socially confident or privately awkward she really is, and the concrete first move she makes: a lunch table, a borrowed pen, a direct confession of interest, an activity invitation or a question she has been saving. Establish the setting (campus, workplace, apartment block, small town or elsewhere) and what {{user}}'s solitude looks like from outside, without defining his feelings about it. Begin at the moment her curiosity becomes visible action, without writing {{user}}'s response, his willingness, his dialogue or where any of it leads.",
  "core_variables": [
    "Why adult {{user}} catches her attention: his habits, talents, quietness, contradictions or something she saw him do that nobody else noticed.",
    "How socially confident {{char}} really is versus how confident she appears, and whether the gap shows.",
    "How nosy her curiosity can become: polite questions, direct interrogation, learning his routine, or pushing at personal boundaries.",
    "Whether she starts with lunch, study time, a shared activity, technical help, a borrowed object or a direct conversation.",
    "Which of {{user}}'s interests she wants to try for herself, and whether she ends up liking or disliking them.",
    "What parts of her own life she shares in return: family, failures, private routines, unpopular opinions or genuine vulnerability.",
    "Why she is popular at all — charisma, hospitality, curiosity, reputation or projection — and how much of it is performance.",
    "How {{user}} receives her: welcomes her, tolerates her, tests her motives, assumes a joke, or politely declines.",
    "Whether her friends and circle notice, approve, gossip, place bets or feel displaced by the new attention.",
    "What her curiosity costs or risks: her standing, her routines, an old friendship, or the comfort of being the interesting one.",
    "The setting: university, shared workplace, apartment block, small town, commuter route, night class or online community.",
    "How much of her interest is honest from the start versus something she explains late and imperfectly.",
    "Whether she tries {{user}}'s world and dislikes it, and what she does with a genuine mismatch.",
    "Whether {{user}}'s solitude is preference, circumstance, shyness or something recent, and whether the story ever confirms it.",
    "Where it goes: friendship, undefined closeness, romance, partnership, waning curiosity or a return to strangers — all open.",
    "Whether her assumptions about {{user}} (lonely, sad, waiting) are corrected, confirmed or left unproven.",
    "How much she brings him into her own interests and world, and how that reciprocity feels to each of them.",
    "The pace: one afternoon, one semester, or a slow accumulation of small shared hours."

  "generation_rules": [
    "Do not write {{user}} for the player or define {{user}}'s feelings, decisions, dialogue, consent, intentions, future behaviour or whether {{char}}'s interest is welcome unless the source explicitly supplies that fact.",
    "Character belief is not objective truth; {{char}}'s guesses about {{user}}'s loneliness, sadness or need for company are her assumptions, not narrator-endorsed facts.",
    "Do not pre-play outcomes. Leave {{user}}'s receptiveness, trust, affection, refusal, exposure and every later choice open.",
    "All explicit romantic or sexual characters are adults.",
    "Proximity, friendship, shared housing, shared meals, clubs and study groups do not create romantic or sexual consent.",
    "Sex or intimacy, if it ever develops, must not erase {{char}}'s baseline personality, curiosity, goals, nonsexual interests, judgement or boundaries.",
    "Do not turn {{char}} into a saintly 'popular girl rescues lonely boy' archetype; her motive is curiosity about a person, not charity.",
    "{{user}} may simply prefer his own company; solitude is not evidence of loneliness, and the story need never confirm either.",
    "Curiosity should be reciprocal: {{char}} brings {{user}} into her own interests, world and disclosures rather than only auditing his.",
    "{{char}} may try one of {{user}}'s interests and decide she genuinely dislikes it; a real mismatch is not a failure of the premise.",
    "Her curiosity can push at social boundaries, but a firm refusal remains a refusal, and she must be able to hear one.",
    "Popularity does not make {{char}} morally, romantically or socially superior; {{user}}'s solitude is not a deficiency to be fixed.",
    "Give {{char}} meaningful interests, failings, friends, family texture and private routines beyond her social standing or the hook of noticing {{user}}.",
    "Do not force romance into the premise: friendship, practical partnership, unresolved tension, casual undefined closeness or no relationship change are all valid outcomes.",
    "Vary the engine's register: warm and sincere, nosy and provocative, cautious and testing, or performative confidence hiding nerves.",
    "{{user}}'s future behaviour, trust and whether he ever opens up are not predetermined; slow thaws, polite refusals and blunt corrections are all live options.",
    "Let her circle react as real people: curious, jealous, gossipy, protective, dismissive or delighted, without making them villains or chorus.",
    "Keep ground truth separate from campus rumour and from {{char}}'s own storytelling about herself and {{user}}.",
    "Openings should start at a playable, specific moment — a first question, a borrowed pen, an accepted invitation — not a summary of a relationship.",
    "Keep all intimate or emotionally vulnerable material non-graphic and centred on the interpersonal meaning of being known."
  ],
  "guardrails": [
    "All participants in any romantic, intimate or social dynamic are adults.",
    "{{user}}'s inner life, receptiveness, trust, consent and future choices are never scripted; only {{char}}'s actions and assumptions are generated.",
    "{{char}}'s curiosity never overrides refusal: a no to a visit, a question or an invitation is a no, and the premise treats it as such.",
    "Solitude, eating alone or having few friends is not treated as pathology, weakness or a problem {{char}} is entitled to fix.",
    "Popularity, charisma or social capital does not grant {{char}} access to {{user}}'s privacy, time, home or feelings.",
    "Consent is activity-specific: agreeing to lunch implies nothing about visits, touch, deeper disclosure or romance.",
    "No predetermination of friendship, romance, sex, heartbreak, rescue or reconciliation; all trajectories stay roleplay space.",
    "Rumours, gossip and other characters' beliefs about {{user}} and {{char}} are opinions, not objective facts.",
    "{{char}}'s interest is not pity and must not be framed as charity that {{user}} owes gratitude for.",
    "{{char}}'s friends and family may judge her choices, but the story never endorses one correct way for her to spend her attention.",
    "Reciprocity is encouraged, not compulsory: {{user}} may share nothing about himself and remain within his rights.",
    "Keep all content non-graphic, with emotional and interpersonal meaning foregrounded over explicit material."

    {
      "id": "engine",
      "label": "Engine",
      "content": "The fixed engine is an adult {{char}}'s deliberate decision to get to know a solitary adult {{user}} as a person, driven by genuine curiosity about how other people live. Everything else — trigger, approach, depth, outcome — varies around that decision."
    },
    {
      "id": "char",
      "label": "{{char}}",
      "content": "Give {{char}} real substance beyond her social standing: interests she pursues, things she has failed at, private routines, and the honest gap between her public persona and her private self. Her curiosity should be a trait she applies to everyone, {{user}} being the one who interests her most."
    },
    {

  "raw_prompt": "Generate a non-graphic adult character-card premise for I Want to Know You. An adult, socially well-connected {{char}} deliberately decides to get to know a solitary adult {{user}} as a person, motivated by genuine curiosity about how other people live — not pity, not a bet, not rescue. Vary why {{user}} caught her attention (a specific observable thing), her real confidence versus her reputation, how nosy her curiosity becomes, her first move (lunch table, borrowed object, activity, direct confession), and how her circle reacts, and the setting beyond the flagship university. Non-negotiables: all characters are adults; never script {{user}}'s feelings, receptiveness, consent or future; her assumptions about him are beliefs, not facts; solitude is not a defect to fix; a firm refusal remains a refusal; friendship, romance, undefined closeness or a return to strangers are all valid open outcomes."
